newsitem.title: UK: U.S. stocks little changed in London trading.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks little changed in London trading.

text.p: U.S. stocks were little changed in London on Wednesday, with markets on hold for today's Beige Book economic review from the Federal Reserve and key inflation pointers later in the week, traders here said.

Traders said the market was due a pause, after gains earlier this month propelled the Dow back to near its record highs set in May. "It's a wait-and-see day," said one, "a pause for breath is probably justified."

Traders said technology stocks were marked higher after the latest book-to-bill report on the state of demand in the semiconductor industry, with some saying the report was slightly better than expected.
The book-to-bill report was issued after the U.S. market closed yesterday and showed the index rose to 0.90 in August from an upwardly revised 0.86 in July.
Expectations for the index, which measures new orders against shipments, had been between 0.86 and 0.92.
Among leading semiconductor stocks, Texas Instruments was up 1/4 at 45-3/4 and Motorola was up 1/4 at 51, traders said.

Auto stocks were marked lower with Ford down for a second day, off $1/8 at $31-1/2, as concerns about a deal with auto unions added to worries about weak trading in Brazil and Argentina, traders said.

A report in the Wall Street Journal said Ford expects to reach a deal soon on a new contract with the United Automobile Workers Union (UAW) and that it sees wider-than-expected losses in its South American operations.
General Motors, which yesterday said it made a comprehensive labour contract offer to the UAW union, was also marked down $1/8 at $47-3/4.

Traders said other stocks prices were little changed from Tuesday's New York close, with the U.S. long bond quoted down just 1/16 at 95-15/32 and the S&P 500 September futures contract down 0.10 points at 665.00.

Strategists and traders said the market would likely take its lead today from the Fed's Beige Book, to be released at 1600 GMT, and would be looking ahead to U.S. inflation reports Thursday and Friday.

Producer prices on Thursday are expected to show a 0.1 percent rise and consumer prices on Friday are expected to show a rise of 0.2 percent in both the headline figure and the core rate excluding food and energy.
Yet some believe signs of a benign inflation background this week could allay fears about rate prospects and propell the Dow higher.

Yesterday U.S. markets retreated after Fed governor Janet Yellen said the U.S. economy had entered an inflation danger zone, though traders said T-bonds had already discounted a quarter point rise at the Fed's next policy meeting.

Joe Rooney, global strategist at Lehman Brothers in London, said he expected the Fed to tighten before the September 24 policy meeting but that the Fed did not have to progressively tighten from that point.
"We will probably get a 25 basis point, or at most a 50 basis point rise, but short term rates are already at high real levels so the bond market has done quite a lot of the Fed's work," Rooney said.
"The Fed doesn't need an awful lot of additional tightening, and once the bond market starts moving higher I don't think there will be any obstacle to equities."
